newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to discuss leasing oil reserve space to Saudi.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to discuss leasing oil reserve space to Saudi.

text.p: U.S. officials plan to discuss leasing out space in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to Saudi Arabia in a meeting next week with Saudi oil minister Ali Naimi, an Energy Department official said Thursday.
Naimi, traveling to Washington as part of a large Saudi delegation, is due to meet with acting U.S. Energy Secretary Charles Curtis on February 25.

They are expected to talk about the general oil market situation and its impact on Saudi Arabia, leasing of space in the SPR, and positions on international negotiations for a climate change treaty, the Energy Department official said.
The discussion is not expected to include any oil-for-planes exchange, an idea which has been floated in the past but rejected by Washington.
There had been speculation that the Saudi delegation, led by defense minister Prince Sultan, might propose using oil to pay for F-16 jet fighters which the kingdom is looking to buy.
"As far as we understand from the Saudis, they are not bringing anything like that along," the energy official said.
Talks between Curtis and Naimi are expected to be fairly general. "We would like to talk a little about storing (Saudi) oil in the SPR," the official said.

Similar proposals in the past had not advanced because the Saudis and other potential users did not like the fact that under law, all oil in the SPR was under the control of the U.S. president and available only in an emergency.

He said if the United States wanted to fill the 110 million barrels of unused capacity in the SPR storage caverns with other countries' oil, it would have to a find way to ensure that their oil would not be under the control of the U.S. government.
The energy official said discussion on the global climate treaty under negotiation was unlikely to be detailed, but added, "We do have divergent views on that."
In international talks for a global warming accord, the United States is pushing for industrialized countries to have binding carbon emissions caps from 2010 onwards to help slow down global warming.
Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, and other major producers oppose setting binding targets for cutting carbon emissions, which largely come from the burning of fossil fuels.
